The paper addresses RCS reduction for microstrip patch antennas operating at 4.3 GHz with dimensions of 80 mm × 80 mm × 1.6 mm.
Three metamaterial-based antenna designs were proposed: PCM structured, L-structured, and square-structured fractal metamaterial antennas.
The reference patch antenna achieved a bandwidth of 143 MHz, gain of 2.8 dB, and RCS of -27.98 dBsm.
The PCM structured antenna achieved the best RCS reduction at -37.14 dBsm.
The L-structured metamaterial antenna achieved the lowest return loss of -28.28 dB.
The square-structured fractal metamaterial antenna achieved the highest bandwidth of 201.9 MHz.
The L-structured metamaterial antenna demonstrated a 29.37% larger bandwidth than the reference patch antenna.
All proposed antennas use FR4 substrate with relative permittivity of 4.4, loss tangent of 0.025, and thickness of 1.6 mm.
Coaxial feeding with 50Ω impedance matching is used in all antenna designs.
Metamaterials possess negative electromagnetic characteristics including negative relative permittivity, permeability, and refractive index.
The overall RCS is expressed mathematically as σ = |√σ_s + √σ_a e^(jφ)|, combining structural and antenna mode contributions.
Structural mode RCS results from direct scattering off the antenna surface.
Antenna mode RCS results from energy absorption and re-scattering due to impedance mismatches.
The PCM structure uses a chessboard-like arrangement with four sections separated by distance.
Adjacent sections in the PCM structure have reflections with 180° phase shift that cancel each other.
Metamaterial loading reduces antenna size, increases efficiency, reduces surface waves, and minimizes mutual coupling.
Energy Band Gap (EBG) structures act as artificial magnetic conductors (AMC) in specific frequency bands.
Radar Absorption Materials (RAM) convert incident RF energy into heat to reduce scattered energy.
Frequency Selective Structures (FSS) are conventional methods used for RCS reduction alongside EBG structures.
The paper used Ansys® HFSS for antenna simulation and design.
Vector Network Analyzer (VNA) was used to measure return loss of fabricated antennas.
Anechoic chamber measurements were conducted for radiation pattern validation.
The reference antenna return loss was -16.88 dB, improved to -28.28 dB with L-structured metamaterial.
Bandwidth improvements ranged from 143 MHz (reference) to 201.9 MHz (square-structured fractal).
Gain values remained relatively consistent across designs, ranging from 2.8 dB to 3.2 dB, showing marginal increases.
